Sigma DynamixOrder flow guide

Reading the order flow

Four order flow tools show where the volume traded and who was aggressive: VP, PREV, CVD and BIG. On the training and assessment charts they sit in the FLOW bar at the top right; in the Terminal, in the Indicators menu (Volume profile, Prior session levels, Delta / CVD, Big orders). We start with the ORB (opening range), the first levels of the day.

Key level=Authorization. It is the only thing that allows you to trade.
Order flow=Context. Big orders, POC, VAH, VAL and CVD tell you what is happening in the market. They are not entry points.

Once a level has given you an authorization, use these tools to watch how price reacts: on the level itself, or on a return to a POC, a VAH, a VAL or a zone of big orders. If price bounces, you can enter on the bounce. If it breaks, you can enter on the break. The decision is always yours.

ORB · Opening rangeVP · Volume profilePREV · Previous sessionCVD · DeltaBIG · Big ordersPutting it together

Two words to know

Aggressive buyer: someone who buys at market and lifts the offer. Aggressive seller: someone who sells at market and hits the bid. Every contract traded has one of the two. The order flow tools count them.

Everything is revealed at replay time: a minute enters the profile and the delta as it trades, nothing from the future is shown.

ORB Opening range

The ORB is the high and the low of the first 15 minutes of the session (09:30 to 09:45 NY): ORB H and ORB L. Turn it on with the Indicators button of a chart (Other indicators). While the range is forming, the orange line follows the high and the low; at 09:45 they are fixed for the day. ORB H and ORB L are also in your key levels: they can give the authorization.

The opening range is where the first battle of the day took place. Once it is set, the market does one of two things on its edges: it breaks out and travels, or it fails and comes back inside.

Scenario 1 · Break

  • A candle closes beyond ORB H (or ORB L), not just a wick
  • Price holds outside; a return to the edge is defended (the retest)
  • Context that helps (see the next parts): CVD accelerating in the direction of the break, big orders pushing through, price leaving the value area
  • The range was a fight; once it is won, the move often extends by one or more widths of the range

Scenario 2 · Re-entry

  • Price breaks out, but closes back inside the range within a few candles
  • Second attempts fail too: the breakout traders are trapped
  • Context that helps: CVD diverging on the breakout, big orders absorbed at the extreme (hollow bubbles)
  • A failed break often travels across the range, to the middle and then to the opposite edge
Note. The first minutes after a break decide everything: wait for a candle to close beyond the edge, and watch the first return to it. A break that cannot hold the retest is often the start of a re-entry.

VP Volume profile of the session

A horizontal histogram on the right of the chart: how many contracts traded at each price since 09:30 New York. It builds up during the session. It is the most useful tool of the day: its shape tells you where price will slow down and where it will accelerate.

Peaks of volume = a fight

A wide part of the profile is a price where buyers and sellers fought hard. When price comes back there, it usually slows down and hesitates: this is where to watch who wins.

Gaps in the profile = acceleration

A thin part of the profile is a price where little traded: nobody defended it. When price enters a gap, it usually accelerates until it reaches the next peak.

What you see

  • green part of a bar: aggressive buying at that price; red part: aggressive selling
  • POC (point of control): the price with the most volume, the market's "fair price" of the day
  • VAH / VAL: top and bottom of the value area, the zone holding 70 % of the volume

How to read it

  • Price inside the value area: the market is balanced, it tends to rotate back to the POC
  • Price leaving the value area and holding outside: the market is looking for a new value, moves can extend
  • Between two peaks, the gap is the path: price tends to travel fast from one peak to the next
  • A wick is not acceptance. A single trade beyond a VAH, a VAL or a level proves little. Price that holds beyond it for several candles, and builds volume there, has been accepted

PREV Previous session

The profile of the previous session (09:30 to 16:00 NY), drawn in pink on the left, with its three levels as pink dashed lines: pPOC, pVAH, pVAL. When one of them is off screen, a small tag at the right edge shows its price and an arrow (▲ above, ▼ below).

  • Opening inside yesterday's value area: expect rotation between pVAL and pVAH
  • Opening outside: watch the first return to pVAH or pVAL. Accepted back inside → the move often travels to the pPOC. Rejected → the move away usually continues
  • pPOC, pVAH and pVAL are frequently tested: treat them like any other key level

Virgin POCs (nPOC)

With PREV on, the chart also shows, in purple dotted lines, the POCs of the sessions before that price has not come back to since: the virgin POCs (or naked POCs, nPOC). Each one is labelled with its day, for example nPOC Tue 20. Up to five sessions back are checked.

  • A POC becomes virgin when the following sessions never trade at its price. As soon as a later session (09:30 to 16:00 NY) touches it, the line is erased
  • Only the regular session counts: a touch during the night or after 16:00 does not erase it
  • Yesterday's POC is always shown as pPOC; the nPOCs are the older ones still untouched

A magnet

An untouched POC is a price where the market agreed a lot and never came back to check. Price is often drawn back to it, especially when it sits in the direction of the move or in a gap of the profile. Use it as a target or a zone to watch.

A reaction zone

On the first touch, price often pauses or pulls back, then decides. It does not mean a reversal. The closest and most recent nPOCs matter most; those older than a week are weak.

Note. A virgin POC is a target, not an authorization. Trade it only if a key level gives you the authorization; then the nPOC helps you choose where to take profits or where to expect a pause.

CVD Delta and cumulative delta

A band at the bottom of the chart. Delta (bars) = aggressive buying minus aggressive selling in each candle: green above zero, red below. CVD (blue line) = the running total of the delta since 09:30 NY. The two dotted lines are the highest and lowest CVD of the opening range (09:30 to 09:45).

Confirmation

Price and CVD rise together: buyers are pushing the move. Price and CVD fall together: sellers are. The move is healthy.

Divergence

Price makes a new high but the CVD does not (or a new low without the CVD): fewer aggressive traders behind the move. Not a signal by itself, but a warning that the move is tiring, especially at a key level.

BIG Big orders

A bubble on the candle at the price where an unusually large aggressive order traded. The number is its size in contracts. The menu next to BIG sets the minimum size shown (≥20, ≥30, ≥50, ≥100): raise it to keep only the largest.

What a big order means: a lot of volume traded at that place. Nothing more. It tells you a price is important to the market right now, not which way price will go.

It can reinforce a break

Big orders on a level that gives way: the volume pushed through and the move can extend. A break of a level backed by big orders is a strong break.

It can mark a reversal

Big buyers do not mean price will explode upwards. Their orders can be absorbed by sellers waiting at that price, and the market turns. The same for big sellers at a low.

aggressive buyer aggressive seller filled = price moved its way in the next 30 s hollow = absorbed, price did not move its way pale = still under watch (30 s)

So do not read a bubble as "buy" or "sell". Read it as "a lot happened here", then watch how price reacts when it comes back to that zone: does it hold and bounce, or does it go through?

Note. For past days, Rithmic does not say which side each trade was on: the side of a big order is estimated from the price move, within the exact buy and sell totals of each price and minute. Read single bubbles with care; several bubbles at the same price are more meaningful.

Putting it together

The order of things never changes:

  1. The key level gives the authorization. No authorization, no trade, whatever the order flow shows.
  2. The order flow gives the context. Where is the POC, the VAH, the VAL, yesterday's levels? Were there big orders near the level? Is the CVD following the price?
  3. Price gives the answer. Watch the reaction on the level, or on a return to a POC, a VAH, a VAL or a big-order zone. It bounces: you can enter on the bounce. It breaks: you can enter on the break.
  4. You decide. Direction, entry, stop and take profits are your call. These tools help you read the market; they never take the decision for you.
Around the levelPoints to a bouncePoints to a break
Big ordersBig orders hit the zone and price does not go through (hollow bubbles)Big orders hit the zone and price goes through and holds
CVDPrice tests the level, the CVD does not follow (divergence)The CVD accelerates in the direction of the break
ProfileLevel on a volume peak, a VAH, VAL or POC (today's or yesterday's) that holdsPrice breaks into a gap of the profile, or leaves the value area and stays outside
nPOCFirst touch of a virgin POC: a pause or a pullback is commonUntouched nPOC in the direction of the break: a natural target
ORBBreak of ORB H or ORB L that closes back inside the range (re-entry)Candle closes beyond the edge and the retest holds

Hints, not signals: one of them alone proves nothing. Keep the chart simple, turn on one or two tools at a time.

Also useful: the VWAP

The VWAP (Indicators menu) is the average price of the day weighted by volume, reset at 09:30 NY. Above it, buyers have the upper hand on average; below it, sellers. Like the POC, it is a price the market tends to come back to, and a level that is often defended on the first return.
